title: Introducing Yourself
pronunciation_focus_summary: The rolled R — the hallmark of Italian pronunciation. The tongue-tip trill appears in mi chiamo, arrivederci, piacere, and countless essential words. Learning to produce it (or approximate it) is key to being understood.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'ch' before 'i' is a hard 'k' sound in Italian. 'Chiamo' is two syllables: KYAH-moh. The 'i' after 'ch' is not a separate syllable — it just signals the hard 'k'.
Both 'o' vowels are closed. Clean, simple pronunciation. Used for nationality, profession, or identity: 'Sono americano', 'Sono insegnante'.
Stress on the first syllable: AH-bee-toh. The 't' is dental — touch your tongue to your upper teeth, not the ridge behind them like in English.
The 'ng' combination is like in English 'finger'. The 'g' is hard. Clean, two syllables for 'vengo'.
Three syllables: pyah-CHEH-reh. The 'c' before 'e' is 'ch' as in 'church'. The final 'e' is always pronounced. Say this while shaking hands.
Formal form using 'si' (oneself, formal). 'Chiama' has a hard 'k' sound. In informal settings, use 'Come ti chiami?'.

phrases.translation: How old are you? (formal, lit. 'How many years do you have?')
phrases.pronunciation_notes: Double 'n' in 'anni' — hold the 'n' longer. The 'h' in 'ha' is completely silent in Italian. 'Qu' is always 'kw'.

phrases.translation: I am thirty years old (lit. 'I have thirty years')
phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'h' in 'ho' is silent. 'Trent'anni' elides — the words flow together with a double 'n' sound. Italian expresses age with 'avere' (to have), not 'essere' (to be).
phrases.example_sentence: Ho trent'anni e abito a Milano.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The rolled 'r' in 'parlo' is important. 'Po'' has an apostrophe because it is shortened from 'poco'. 'Italiano' has five syllables with stress on 'a'.
phrases.example_sentence: Mi scusi, parlo un po' di italiano.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Negation is simple — put 'non' before the verb. 'L'italiano' elides because 'italiano' starts with a vowel. Practice the rolled 'r' in 'parlo'.
phrases.example_sentence: Mi dispiace, non parlo bene l'italiano.

phrases.pronunciation_notes: Adjectives change ending based on gender: '-o' for masculine, '-a' for feminine. The 'r' in 'americano' should be tapped or rolled.
The rolled 'r' in 'parla'. 'Inglese' has a hard 'g' and the 's' between vowels is voiced like 'z'. No question word needed — just raise intonation at the end.
The 'sc' before 'o' is a hard 'sk' sound (not 'sh' — that only happens before 'e' or 'i'). Stress on the second syllable: ka-PEE-sko.
phrases.example_sentence: Mi scusi, non capisco. Puo ripetere?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: The 'uo' in 'puo' is a diphthong, one syllable. 'Ripetere' has four syllables with stress on 'pe'. Two rolled 'r' sounds to practice.
phrases.example_sentence: Non capisco. Puo ripetere, per favore?

phrases.pronunciation_notes: 'Che' is 'keh' — the 'ch' in Italian is always a hard 'k'. 'Lavoro' has a clear 'v' and rolled 'r'. Simple rising intonation for the question.
The 'gn' in 'insegnante' is a palatal nasal, like 'ny' in 'canyon'. Double 'n' sound in the 'gn'. No article needed with professions after 'sono'.
More formal than just 'piacere'. The 'sc' before 'e' is a 'sh' sound. Double 'sh' in 'conoscerLa'. 'La' (capitalized) refers to the formal 'you'.
Informal form using 'sei' (you are, informal). 'Dove' has a closed 'o'. The diphthong 'ei' in 'sei' sounds like 'ay' in 'say'.

dialogues.context: Meeting a colleague at a business conference

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.translation: Good morning, my name is Sarah.

exchanges.speaker: colleague
exchanges.text: Piacere, mi chiamo Roberto. Di dov'e?
exchanges.translation: Nice to meet you, my name is Roberto. Where are you from?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: pyah-CHEH-reh mee KYAH-moh roh-BEHR-toh dee doh-VEH

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Vengo da New York. E Lei?
exchanges.translation: I come from New York. And you?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: VEHN-goh dah New York eh LAY

exchanges.speaker: colleague
exchanges.text: Sono di Roma. Che lavoro fa?
exchanges.translation: I'm from Rome. What work do you do?
exchanges.phonetic_approx: SOH-noh dee ROH-mah keh lah-VOH-roh fah

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Sono insegnante. Parlo un po' di italiano.
exchanges.translation: I'm a teacher. I speak a little Italian.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: SOH-noh een-seh-NYAHN-teh PAHR-loh oom POH dee ee-tah-LYAH-noh

dialogues.notes: In business settings, always use Lei (formal you) until invited to use tu. Italians appreciate any effort to speak Italian, even imperfectly.

dialogues.context: Meeting a friend's friend at a casual dinner

exchanges.speaker: friend
exchanges.text: Questa e la mia amica, Laura.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: KWEH-stah eh lah MEE-ah ah-MEE-kah LOW-rah

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Ciao Laura, piacere! Mi chiamo Alex.
exchanges.translation: Hi Laura, nice to meet you! My name is Alex.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: CHOW LOW-rah pyah-CHEH-reh mee KYAH-moh Alex

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Sono americano. Abito a Roma da un anno.
exchanges.translation: I'm American. I've been living in Rome for a year.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: SOH-noh ah-meh-ree-KAH-noh AH-bee-toh ah ROH-mah dah oon AHN-noh

dialogues.notes: When introduced through a mutual friend, it is normal to switch to 'tu' immediately, especially among people of similar age. Italians love to compliment foreigners who try to speak Italian.

exchanges.speaker: you
exchanges.text: Ciao! Parlo un po' di italiano.
exchanges.translation: Hi! I speak a little Italian.
exchanges.phonetic_approx: CHOW PAHR-loh oom POH dee ee-tah-LYAH-noh

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.translation: Very good! How old are you?

exchanges.speaker: other
exchanges.translation: Me too! Do you speak other languages too?

dialogues.notes: 'Bravissimo' is the superlative of 'bravo' — Italians use it generously as encouragement. 'Anch'io' (me too) is a very useful phrase to learn early.

cultural_notes.title: Titles matter in Italian culture
cultural_notes.content: Italians use professional titles much more than English speakers. A doctor is 'Dottore/Dottoressa' (and this includes anyone with a university degree, not just medical doctors). A lawyer is 'Avvocato', an engineer 'Ingegnere', a professor 'Professore/Professoressa'. Using someone's title shows respect. In formal introductions, you might hear 'Piacere, sono il Dottor Rossi' rather than just a first name. When unsure, 'Signore' (Mr.) and 'Signora' (Mrs./Ms.) are always safe.

cultural_notes.title: Italians ask personal questions — it's friendly, not nosy
cultural_notes.content: Don't be surprised if Italians you've just met ask about your age, marital status, family, or salary. These topics aren't considered invasive in Italian culture — they're signs of genuine interest and warmth. Questions like 'Sei sposato/a?' (Are you married?) or 'Hai figli?' (Do you have children?) are standard small talk. Feel free to answer or deflect politely, but know it comes from a place of friendliness.
